utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I do understand that the Prosecution has at least one urgent replacement of a translation in e-court. If you could deal with that one and leave the others until later.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This relates to the English translation for P1657 and P1658.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And there was a handwritten word, "Mladic," on the top of the page that was missing from the translation, and the revised English translation has been uploaded under document ID --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you're now dealing with 1657 or 1658?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: 0086-9333-A-ET. And if the Defence have no objection, we'd request that this English revised translation replace the existing one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have no objection to the translation. We wonder why we have two of the exact same in e-court. That's a matter for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a look at it. Madam Registrar, you're hereby instructed to replace the English translation of P1657 and P1658 by the document just referred to by Ms. Hasan, and I noted that the number accurately appears on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jevdjevic. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you again, hopefully for the last time, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Hasan will now continue her cross-examination. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we take a look at P1397 under seal, page 2 in the English and page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You'll recall that we were a looking at an intercept from the 2nd of August at 0950 hours in the morning. We'll just continue where we left off. And if you look at about three quarters of the way down the page, and in the English, I think we left off where Obrenovic asks to talk to Jevdjevic for a moment, and the -- the telephone is passed on to Jevdjevic, and the communication continues. Now, just towards the end of the English, we see Obrenovic say: "Which road should I uses to send a truck in your direction to pick up some cattle?" I had asked you about what that was a reference to. And Jevdjevic responds: "And where is that? "Obrenovic: Well, I don't know. My boss told me to give you a call because you know where most of them are." And if we turn in the page in the English, Jevdjevic responds: "Well, the others have already grabbed everything." "Obrenovic: And there's nothing left, huh? "Jevdjevic: Not really. "Obrenovic: The motherfuckers are worse than termites. "Jevdjevic: Even worse. Now their code-names are Cowboy 1 and Cowboy 2." And then there's some laughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 in the B/C/S and stay with the English, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The conversation continues and at the top of that page, Jevdjevic says: "They're in a place where Legenda often carried out searches." And then further up, Obrenovic: "So should I go to Milici?" "Jevdjevic: Podravanje and up to Stublic." And Jevdjevic confirms: "You'll find them at Stublic." So, Mr. Jevdjevic, do you recall this discussion about the transportation of cattle that were in the Podravanje and Stublic area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have a document, 65 ter 32087. Let's see if this helps refresh your recollection. What this is, is -- it's from the assistant commander for logistics at the Drina Corps, Colonel Lazar Acamovic, and it's dated the 5th of August, so a few days after the intercepted conversation. And it's to be delivered to the Visegrad Brigade Bratunac, the Milici, and the Vlasenica Brigades. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the document on the screen, I can't see that list of addressees. There's no Zvornik, Milici, and Vlasenica Brigade. It's an authorisation issued to a person to do certain things, and the units that you quoted are not mentioned in this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you are not on the right page of the document. Please check that, Ms. Hasan. Oh, it's the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. 32088.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then you misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It said 32 --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: 087. I see that on the record. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now looking at the screen I do that this is the correct one. And what this is, it's a telegram -- it says: "Pursuant to a telegram of the Main Staff from 4 August 1995, send us information about the number and sort of collected cattle from the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa by 0200 [sic] hours on 5 August 1995." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, but this document is not related to the Zvornik Brigade as you claim it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I had mentioned the Zvornik Brigade, then it's clear that this is not one of the addressees. But in terms of the content, the subject matter of this telegram where the Main Staff is requesting information about the cattle gathered in the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never had anything to do with the collection of cattle as part of my job. My job was to deal with communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd offer 65 ter 32087 -- 88 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32088 will be Exhibit P7143.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And could we now have 32087 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And this is the document we were looking at previously. And it's from General Krstic, dated the 5th of August, and it's an authorisation for Cvijetin Micic from the Zvornik Brigade to collect and transport to Zvornik the abandoned cattle from the former enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and it's pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff and the commander of the Drina Corps 17 July 1995. Now in the intercept at 0950 hours, Obrenovic is asking you about where to send the truck to pick up the cattle. So do these documents then now help you remember the discussion you were having with Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bring back the intercepted conversation on the screen. You'll see that Obrenovic is talking to a person called Vidoje, not Jevdjo. Bring back the conversation and you will see that clearly for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we look at P01397 under seal, and I would also offer 32088 -- sorry, -87 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32087 will be Exhibit P7144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And we see here and you're referring to - B/C/S page 2, please, and English page 2 - after Obrenovic says: "Can I take to Jevdjevic for a moment?" Krstic says: "Jevdjevic." Obrenovic says: "Yes." Krstic says: "All right." And he says: "I'll put him on." And then X, who is identified as Jevdjevic at the beginning of this intercept, says: "Hello." Obrenovic then, and this is what you're referring to, says: "(Vitoje?)" This is what you're referring to; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a question. This is the way the person addresses his interlocutor, by using his first name. It is in brackets with a question mark, and my interpretation of that is this: My nickname was never Vitoje, nobody ever called me that, which means that Obrenovic is calling a person called Vitoje who says yes, and then he says listen, and the conversation continues then. Since I do not remember that I ever took care of any cattle, that I was never Vitoje -- even at previous trials I testified that I don't remember that conversation as a conversation that I was involved in. In the same intercepted conversation intercepted from a different location, and we mentioned the north and the south locations, entirely different wordings are mentioned in respect of this conversation. The same conversation was intercepted at the same time from a different location and in that intercept it says that Obrenovic actually inquires where he should bring a lorry full of cattle, whereas in this conversation on the screen, it seems that he is asking where he can bring a lorry to fetch the cattle. You can compare the two conversations or intercepts, and the difference will become abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you are engaging in analysing what you consider to be the evidence. What we'd like to know is what you remember, and you say, and that's clear, I was not the one -- at least you don't remember to have conducted this conversation. That is good enough. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we can just turn to page 1 in the English and 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You will see that this communication was picked up on frequency 255.950, which is within the range of a RRU-1. Now, this is the device you were using at Zlovrh; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were using that device, but I'm not sure about the frequency and I've already said that several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We have this intercepted communication on audiotape. We have it from the northern facility, and we have it from the southern facility. From the northern facility, we hear Obrenovic more clearly than the other participants, and in the southern facility, we hear Krstic more clearly. Now, I don't have much time to play both, but I will play the one where we hear Krstic and Jevdjevic, which -- it's our position that that's you in that conversation clearly on that tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So could we take a look at 65 ter 21235e.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And there is an interception where all the participants are picked up on the one frequency. And it's to address your testimony from yesterday where you said that -- where both -- where participants are picked up on one frequency, one participant is barely heard or cannot be heard at all. So let's listen to that audio.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart corrects me. It's 21235f for that audio. And, Your Honours, there is a transcript for the audiotape which can be displayed on the screen. But for the purposes of the exercise of just hearing the voices, I would request that we receive no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, I take it that for these purposes it's acceptable that we leave out any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I would ask that the volume on the devices be turned up as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jevdjevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Jevdjevic be assisted to have his volume at the highest level. Or at least at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Him being a technician himself, he will be able to -- Mr. Jevdjevic, if you would need higher volume or lower, then you'll find the buttons there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And let me just put on the record the -- okay. This is just the clip so I don't think we need the time code.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, were you able to hear the voices of all the participants?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very well. I heard this conversation in 2000 or 2001 when I testified in the Krstic case, and it seems to me that the quality of the audio was better at the time. All of you who have listened to this conversation now and who have been following my testimony would never confirm that it was me speaking because now they know how I speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are -- again, you're not invited to give your analysis of the evidentiary situation. You're here to answer the questions put to you by Ms. Hasan, and you told us that you said that the voices were difficult to hear. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, this communication which was intercepted by the ABiH is an authentic communication, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer 21235f into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you -- before that will be admitted, I have a question for the witness. Did you recognise any of the voices of the speakers we have listened to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really did not. There's a huge modulation. I'm sure that you all heard that, a huge modulation of the voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You didn't recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only assume that it is the two of them. But when I listen carefully, the modulation is huge, and the voices are so distorted that they don't resemble anybody's voice. The tone of their voices is so distorted, and I'm sure that you could all hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, has the transcript been verified by CLSS? That would be my concern since we did not have translation of the audio.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm told that the transcript has not been verified by CLSS ahead of time, but we could play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I wonder whether it's the task of CLSS to do this job on the spot. Therefore, I would suggest that you find a more quiet way of -- for CLSS to verify the transcript. Are there any specific concerns, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't open it here to be able to check. That's why I asked. So I've been working without the transcript of that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And why is it that it can be not opened? Is it uploaded in e-court? And what then is the problem? Under what number?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It's the same 65 ter number which is 21235f.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's what I've plugged in and it's not coming up at my end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With the caveat that I have been computer issues all morning, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On 21235f, I get an audio intercept, a B/C/S translation and an English translation. If I open the English translation, I get an English transcript text. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which is the one that we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Let me see. Yes, it is exactly the same as we have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then there is an issue because there's a word missing. It's the second-to-last line in the English that's on the screen right now. It's not on the B/C/S, but the word that was spoken by the individual on the tape at that point has not been recorded on this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean between "hello" and "yes"? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Could we scroll down in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that should be the critical point that the witness has pointed out, that another name was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Approximately at the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Here the B/C/S is not giving any ... So, therefore, if the Defence takes the position that although so badly audible all of this, that this can be deciphered in audio terms, then, of course, I take it that perhaps the Prosecution with one of the language assistants and the Defence could sit together and see whether they can fill in what is here recorded as inaudible. I take it that's what the dots stands.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What that means is that the person who did this transcript was not able to hear that. We can have them listen to it again and verify that they can hear it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could ask the Defence as well. If they've good ears and if your people have good ears, then you can sit together. It's not necessarily that if one person of CLSS is unable to hear it or decipher it that others could not assist in this exercise. And, Mr. Ivetic, is it -- because you pointed at the dots in the English version, whereas in the original it seems that it's declared more or less by the person working on it as inaudible. Did you have an opportunity or were you able or were one of your colleagues able to hear what would have been said?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, in listening -- in listening in court it sounded to me like Vitoje, but of course I'm not a native speaker and I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that the -- well, at least you have a --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour we can listen to it again with the Defence and see if it's audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's proceed like that. As matters stand now, we have this version, which is made, I take it, to the best of the abilities of the transcriber. We have to deal with this at this very moment, and if there would be any better version in the near future, we'll hear from the parties. Now let me just check whether it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 21235f will receive number P7145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7145 is admitted into evidence. But the Chamber explicitly states that if the parties agree on a better transcript version, whereas, the audio is part of this evidence as well, that the transcript, of course, that parties could apply for the transcript to be replaced by a better one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could with take a look at 32120.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, in 2003, late 2003 and early 2004, the Office of the Prosecutor interviewed Dragan Obrenovic, and a statement was produced, a witness statement of his, signed witness statement. And if we can look at -- we see the cover page appearing on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I think we're missing the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: There you see that's the cover page of Obrenovic's witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we can now turn to page 21 in the English and page 30 in the B/C/S. Can we take a look at paragraph 157.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You will see there's a heading. It says: "Intercept," dated 2nd August, 1995, between Krstic Obrenovic. And paragraph 157 states: "I have listened to an intercepted conversation, dated 2 August 1995, at 0950 hours, between myself, General Krstic, and Major Jevdjevic. The conversation was played as part of a videotape which carried the sound of this intercept." And then he goes on at paragraph 158.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we turn the page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: "I have already listened to this intercept some time ago together with my lawyers. I did tell them at that time and I ... confirm it now again that this is my own voice and the one of General Krstic." You see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you still contest that this is an authentic intercept?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the part of the conversation that has to do with me. I do not remember it because it is not consistent with the actual situation that I participated in. And my name is recorded as something completely different in that conversation. That is the part that I have been referring to. Even if that were so, I was not at General Krstic's at the time. I was at the communications centre and he was at the observation post at the forward command post, but I'm speaking about the part of that conversation where I have allegedly taken part. *Q. Let's move on. You testified about the Croatians's ability to intercept VRS communications, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think if we would go into any further details, we may have to move into private session, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we -- I don't know what details you further want to address.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I think for the time being we can stay in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we call up 65 ter 27618. This is an under-seal document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What will appear before you, Witness, is an intercept dated 16 July 1995 at 2235 hours. It is a conversation between General Mladic and Milos Kostic. Now, if we just look at the beginning of that intercept, we see M, General Mladic, saying: "Good evening, Brother Kostic." It's line 8 in the English. *And this is a conversation where they are discussing Gorazde, Zepa, amongst other things. If we turn to page 2 in the English, and I'll direct you, Witness, to about two-thirds of the way down the page, lines 32 in the English, Mladic says: "I understood you completely, Milos. You said all of it well; the best thing would be that they give up on the Muslims and Croats." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So let's turn to the English page 3. The conversation continues. And at line 16, this is Milos -- this is Milos Kostic speaking, and he says: "That supposedly is the case. That's what these guys are forecasting of the UN. Again, it was reported here that you stopped at 1.5 kilometres from Zepa but that is not the case, it seems. Has Zepa been completed, Boss?" Do you say that? It's towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, just a few lines, about six lines -- six or seven lines from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mladic responds: "Well, all right, one chases that around." So -- sorry. Mladic responds: "It has been completed, mate. There are just some smaller groups still." *"Kostic: Well, all right, one chases that around." "Mladic: Of course, you just do your job and do not worry." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And we're going to turn now to P01658, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you'll see there's a communication -- this is a record from the security service centre. It's an intercepted communication, and it's the communication numbered 672. So the second one in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we turn one page in the English, we will see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And we see that it says: "On the same day on the same frequency, and the same channel at 2250 hours, we recorded a conversation between Ratko Mladic and Cvijetin Kostic, who was inaudible." Now, this communication was picked up a bit later than that picked up by the Croatians, but what they record is the conversation from Mladic's side, and what they hear is: "How are you Kostic?" And if we look just two lines -- three lines down, Mladic says: "The best thing would be to give up on the Muslims completely and on the Croats as well." The next thing we hear -- they hear Mladic say is: "That's finished, bro. There are only some smaller groups left." We skip a line, we go to the next one: *"You just do your job and don't worry." And Mladic continues. So, sir, we have now looked at a communication that has been intercepted by the Croatians and intercepted by the security service centre on the same date at approximately the same time. Now, you do acknowledge that the Croatians were able to intercept communications, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you put that question more precisely, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, we've just looked at two intercepts, and on the basis of what you've seen here, was it possible for the Croatians to intercept communications?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you're asking the witness whether, on the basis of what we see here, whether it was possible. Of course, that's asking for a judgement or opinion of the witness. The question is whether, having looked at this, whether it's still your evidence that they could not intercept communications or do you accept that they could? I take it that that's the question, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the clarification. In my testimony a few days ago, I said in my professional assessment because of the specific position and the geographic location of the relay communications of the Drina Corps, that I do not believe that the Croats could successfully listen to these conversations. This *is the Pale relay communication which is not in the zone and does not belong to the communications of the Drina Corps, and I don't know what was meant. The Pale route that was listened to by the Croats - that is to say, the people from the Tuzla security centre - does not belong to the Drina Corps. It is more towards Central Bosnia. That is to say, in that schematic of the radio relay communications of the Drina Corps, you will not find a Pale route anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you acknowledge that this intercept, which was picked up by the Croatians, is authentic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it corresponds to the actual situation and if there are other indicators, I'm not challenging it. I don't know what this is all about. I am not well versed in what was going on, so I cannot assert that it is authentic. If you have information stating that it is authentic, it is probably authentic. However, it was intercepted outside the zone of the Drina Corps and that is what I have been testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd offer 65 ter 27618 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness has been unable to offer any evidence about this intercept to either confirm, et cetera, and it goes -- it's not been authenticated by other means, as far as I know, to be able to be to be introduced at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan. *MS. HASAN: Well, the witness has said that he doesn't challenge the authenticity and said if you have information stating it is authentic it's probably authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Ms. Hasan, if a witness comes and says I have no reason to challenge the authenticity, would that in itself be a reason? Then everyone in this world who does not know anything about this, and, of course, could not challenge the authenticity, not having any knowledge, would be a good witness so as to introduce this document through him or her. Is that your position or is there more to be said about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, is he able to comment. I mean, he's been shown and it's been compared to the -- the -- the same intercept being picked up by the State Security Service, and that in itself he can opine and has opined on the -- whether -- whether this is made up by the State Security Service and the Croatians or not. And I can -- I can just add that -- oh, I'll just leave it at that for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think again it's a question of what this witness has been able to confirm or add useable evidence as to, and I don't think in relation to this document that the testimony we've heard here this morning meets that standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The witness has at length testified about possibilities for intercepts and has gone into some *details in that respect. Now this is put to him and it is relevant evidence, his comment on whether or not he is aware of any facts which would challenge the authenticity of these documents, again, against his background, his professional background. The objection is therefore denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I then, at least for the record, state something to make sure that you're not misrecalling the evidence. The testimony elicited during direct examination was in relation to communications from radio relay nodes in the Drina Corps of which the witness has said that this is going through a node that is outside the Drina Corps, so it does not relate to his prior evidence as to what was possible and not, and I think that's what he's actually said about ten minutes ago in relation to this. So I just wanted to make sure that you had that in mind when making this ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had everything in our mind, including that sometimes the witness testified about the zone of the Drina Corps, sometimes he was testifying about the Drina Corps. He was sometimes testifying about what you could listen -- what you could hear from the various -- the various frequencies used. It is a rather complex thing, Mr. Ivetic, and we'll certainly keep in mind all the details of that testimony further on, and it is on the basis of that testimony as a whole that the objection was denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, therefore, the objection being denied, *Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 27618 receives Exhibit P7146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear, if Mladic on the night of the 16th is in Crna Rijeka, then the communication path is from Crna Rijeka to Veliki Zep and Veliki Zep down to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's argument at this moment and we're hearing the testimony of a witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now you testified that one of UNPROFOR's members, and I'm moving on to another area, was killed, you thought, on the 10th of July. And this is at transcript 31971, lines 15 to 16. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In fact, there's evidence in this case that it was on the 8th of July that Private Rave Van Renssen, an UNPROFOR soldier, was killed. Do you allow for the possibility that your recollection in respect of when the UNPROFOR member was killed does not serve you well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I had information that that had happened on the 10th when their check-point with four APCs in fear of the Muslims went out to the area that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're not invited to recount the whole story but you were asked whether, where you said that you thought it was on the 10th of July, whether you allow for the possibility that you made a mistake and that it would have been on the 8th. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have information that that was on the 10th of July, and I cannot relate to any other date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. And that concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in time, Ms. Hasan, because I had just asked for the time you had used which was, indeed, even a little bit over the last time estimate you gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take a break, Judge Fluegge has one short question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, earlier today, you were asked about this intercept where the term "cattle" appears. Your answer to related question on page 5, line 9 and 10, was, and I quote: "No, I never had anything to do with the collection of cattle as part of my job. My job was to deal with communications." I understand that answer, but have you ever heard that sometimes in communication, radio communication, terms were used which the idea -- terms were used other than those referring to the truth of -- or the real content of the communication? Perhaps "cattle" referred to something else. It was a coded name. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard different coded words that actually referred to something else during the course of the war. However, in this specific conversation, cattle, truck, loading, did not associate me to anything from the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you can't exclude that "cattle" stands for anything else than cattle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of how the conversation went. And the Prosecutor presented evidence to effect that cattle was gathered as war booty. Perhaps in this case it was animals. Sometimes perhaps there were some statements when people referred to the population, the people there, as cattle, livestock, in a pejorative way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then would have one other question for you. Are you aware of the Main Staff directly dealing with the details of the transportation of war booty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We take a break. Mr. Ivetic, your time estimate remains as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I think about 40 minutes should be -- should suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take a break. Witness, you may following the usher, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I missed you -- we move into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I give you an opportunity to re-examine the witness, Mr. Ivetic, I would have one question for the witness. Witness, at some length we have discussed whether you were the interlocutor in that telephone conversation about the -- about the cattle. Now, you also told us that there were other persons with the same family name, Jevdjevic, you are familiar with, or at least you knew about. Could you tell us, is any of those persons with the same family name in a position that you could expect him to participate in such a intercepted conversation? If so, please tell us who you are referring to, what his position was, so that we -- so that we can consider that when evaluating the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may start to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start by returning to P1153 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were questioned about this order from the command of the Drina Corps at transcript page 31980. Now -- and relates to the movements of Legenda with his unit. During the time-period that this activity was under way, where was General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Pribicevac IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where were you during this entire time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also there, at the Pribicevac IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What activities was General Zivanovic undertaking in the course of these activities; that is, the movement of Jolovic and his unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge of the entire activity during the relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now turn to P1417, page 10 in the English, page 17 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, while we wait for that, sir, this is the statement of a Prosecution witness, Mr. Franken, which was also presented to you, and it was represented that the paragraphs from 38 onward relate to this activity that was the subject of the prior order. Now, you were asked about this yesterday -- the other day, and Franken's statement talks of a main battle tank being used at the time at Zeleni Jadar by the VRS. Do you recall if a main battle tank was part of the VRS forces that took part that this activity of relocating from one part to another in Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now the document we just looked at, P1153, we don't have to return to it, but it does not have any instructions for manoeuvring of a tank. Would you expect if a main battle tank is utilized for the order given for a particular activity to give instructions for the unit that is utilizing a main battle tank?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to Prosecution Exhibit P2100, and page 2 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For your recollection, this is the post-action report that is purporting to have your name on it, and I understand that you've already said that the operation was conducted without a single bullet fired and that therefore you would take issue with this part. But if we see here in item number 3, this report says: "We expended small amounts of ammunition and three Zoljas." Do you believe it possible for a main battle tank round or rounds to have been fired near the UNPROFOR check-point without being recorded in such a post-action report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, given where you were while this was going on, do you believe it possible for a main battle tank round to have been fired near the UNPROFOR check-point without you hearing or knowing of the same?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that I would have heard such an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Franken also mentioned some gun on a ridge as was presented to you the other day. Do you think it possible that a gun on a ridge could fire on that area in Zeleni Jadar without being heard by you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cannon round or a round fired from a cannon detonates in the same way as a round from a tank and I'm sure I would have heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have testified that this operation or this activity was undertaken without a single bullet having been fired. In your military career, how common of an occurrence was it for an operation to be completed without a bullet fired?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the operation went that way. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is, by the way, not an answer to the question, Mr. Ivetic. I don't know whether you're seeking a repeated answer to what you didn't ask the witness, then, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe there's something missing from the question [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that's the case, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I better understand why you insist on a repetition. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my war career, I remember that that operation was the only one which was carried out without a bullet being fired, and this is what makes it memorable, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to then move to the meeting that you've testified about on the evening of the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, looking at the document, I think the author is one of the issues very much discussed. Now, I noticed that in the English versions it says "signature," whereas on the original I see the stamp but not any signature. Is that -- now this may happen more often, but especially perhaps in this context it is relevant, that no reference in the English text is to a signature which does not appear in the original. Ms. Hasan, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I see that there, and we will be requesting a revision of that to ensure the record is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, I thought we had -- I think -- I thought one of the Judges had already drawn our attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I must admit that I'd forgotten that. But it could even be me and that I then suggested not to change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any event, it's welcome information and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least I'm consistent on my mind then, apparently. That's -- and if we at the same time said that there's no need to have it corrected, then we leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, turning to the 11 July meeting you spoke of, are there any other factors which stand out in your mind which lead you to believe that the meeting indeed took place on the 11th of July as opposed to any other date?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what other factors stand out in your mind identifying that date as the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, General Mladic, General Krstic, General Zivanovic, and as far as I remember all the brigade commanders, attended the meeting. And when I spoke to them, they all remembered that meeting. At the end of the meeting itself, when General Mladic ordered me, and I remember that order very well, he told me, "You, kid, I want you to set up an IKM at Krivace for the operation in Zepa." That's how the meeting ended. And a certain gentleman, Zvonko Bajagic, appeared on the door-step. He had a platter in his hands with a fish, a carp I believe it was, on that platter. On the 11th of July, that was the last day of the long lent, and Zvonko Bajagic [Realtime transcript read in error "Babic"] is a very religious person. He was in the logistics of the Drina Corps. He wanted to serve those officers food which was considered to be appropriate for fasting. On the following day, we could eat anything. We could eat pork or lamb or anything else. Any kind of meat. This is why I believe - and I'm absolutely certain - that that meeting could have taken place only on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you identify for us which religious holiday is at issue?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saint Peter's Day. In our language it is known as Petrov Dan. On that day, is the day of the -- of a very long fasting period, and after that, you can eat meat. On that note, us officers never received fish. But Zvonko Bajagic is a very religious person, he observed the fasting period, and that's why on that day, the last day of the fasting period, he brought us fish for dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the transcript, page 30, line 25 I believe has "Zvonko Babic," whereas the witness has referred to Zvonko Bajagic, and the remaining references from that point onward have referred to Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to look at D289 with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the very urgent order from General Zivanovic dated 11 July, 1995, and you at transcript page 32046 gave us an explanation of how and why you believe that this was signed by the individual with the time and date indicated here in handwriting. What is the bases or source of your belief that this document was received in Boksanica at the Drina Corps command by Mr. Sekulic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at that time the only place where that telegram could have arrived was at the command post in Vlasenica at its communications centre, because the Pribicevac IKM had been dismantled. Oliver Sekulic, who was in charge of receiving telegrams and who was an encoder, told me that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at now at P7132.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, this is dated the 12th of July, 1995, and we have the handwritten received at 7.40 in the morning. The first question I have for you, the Mr. Mirko Petrovic that is listed in this order -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you, sir, in relation to the handwritten part indicating when it was received, what is the bases of -- the explanation and your bases thereof of how it is that this document shows being received at the date and time indicated?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when my encoder received this document, we were at the corps command in Vlasenica. My encoder, who was in charge of working at the IKM, went to the communications centre and received this telegram in the communications centre. He never switched on his teleprinter that we were using at the forward command post. Up to the afternoon of the 12th of July, we were in Vlasenica and the communications devices and the communications centre were there. The telegrams that were sent to us were received directly from the sender, not through the communications means. That's why I'm saying that this document was printed on the teleprinter which was located at the communications centre in Vlasenica and not on the teleprinter which was in the vehicle which was at the Pribicevac IKM and later on in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could move along to P4895, and I believe this one can be broadcast. And it will be page 38 in the English, page 60 in the Serb, and paragraph 129.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you were asked about these regulations relating to a forward command post in cross-examination. The question I want to ask you: At the moment when you packed up and moved the communications centre from the forward command post at Pribicevac on the 11th of July, 1995, where were the commanding officers of this forward command centre? Did any of them remain at Pribicevac after you left?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them remained at Pribicevac. When I put together the communications centre and started marching, they were already in the Bratunac sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, what is your understanding of the duty of the forward command post communications centre when command officers have moved elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A communications centre and a forward command post follow the battle order, and they follow their units and their commander. It would be impossible and it would be stupid for them to stay behind because they would not be effective. They would not be efficient at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now look at P7131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is also under seal and should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope it's the right document. Ah. Yes, yes, yes. And if we could go to the end of the document, I'd like to focus on the stamp in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the last line of the stamp which is the -- the row that says "delivered," there does not appear to be any information entered as to the day, date, and month, or the hour and minute, nor is it signed. Can we draw any conclusions based upon the lack of any data entered into this part of the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that this telegram was not delivered to all units at this in point in time, 2250. It was not delivered to all the units that it had been intended for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If it had been delivered to all the units, what would you expect to be present?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, the encoder is waiting for the right time to get in touch with each and every unit. And then when even the last units has received this telegram, then he records the time of receipt. Only when the other side confirms to him with a QRV that that is when it was received, at such and such a time, and then he signs it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we return to the first page of this document. Yesterday you were asked in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I think the part that we want is on the -- oh, there it is. If we could scroll up on the English version. Down, sorry, the other direction. It's on the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were asked here about the second sentence in part 1 of the order that says: "Until further notice, ensure that the forward command posts is taken over at all levels of command and control and monitor the situation around-the-clock." Could you identify for us how many levels within the Drina Corps had their own forward command posts according to their formation structure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forward command posts, it is corps, brigades, and battalions that had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the lower-level forward command posts of the brigades and the battalions, who or what officer would establish the same?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the officers from that brigade is always designated, or from these battalions, who was available at that point in time. Usually it would be the operations officer or the chief of staff or the deputy commander of the battalion, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to look at P7134 with you. And, sir, when you were asked about this document yesterday, you highlighted Mr. Mirko Plakalovic and said you did not consider the document to be a -- to be recorded with precision. Can you explain what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Plakalovic was a soldier of mine. And with a mobile device, he always escorted General Krstic in his vehicle, and he was with him. It was only on the 14th of July when the other units were relocated from the area of Srebrenica to the area of Zepa, it was only then, on that day, that from the area of Srebrenica, he came to the area of Zepa. So this information here about him, that cannot be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to move to P1397 - which should not be broadcast - and I'd like to take another look at it with you so that we're clear of what we're talking about. Now, sir, in cross-examination, you testified as to having seen other versions of this purported intercept which had different text. I think you indicated one provided that the cattle was supposed to be sent towards Krstic rather than towards Obrenovic. I'd like to look together with you at P1663, which also should not be broadcast. This is a report from the ABiH purporting to be dated the 2nd of August, 1995. And if we look at the partial translation, the part that's under zone 2, we have again a conversation between General Krstic, Colonel or Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic, and it is at the time of 9.50 in the morning, and it is on the frequency 245.950 megahertz. Now, the first question I have for you, sir: In August of 1995, was Mr. Obrenovic a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel in rank as is reflected on this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge, sir, of what rank Mr. Obrenovic had during the relevant time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could briefly look at 65 ter number 27518. And I think that one is only in the B/C/S. If we could turn to page 6 of the same, this is the financial file of Mr. Obrenovic, at least that's how it's identified by the Prosecution in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at the entries here, and I think even English speakers can see the dates of the entries, but could you please read the effective dates that Obrenovic was a major?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this, Obrenovic was a major until the 31st of December, 1995, when he was promoted to the rank of lieutenant-colonel. And then there's also the order number there, and again the date, the 31st of December, 1995, and the signature of the responsible person that verifies that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does this information as reflected in this document accord with your recollection and knowledge of the dates of Obrenovic's various ranks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to P1663, which again should not be broadcast. You have already in cross-examination told us about some differences in the subject of the conversation, which can be compared from the two documents. I'd like to focus on something you did not mention, which is on page 2 in the English, and it is in the lower quarter of the page in the B/C/S, where Obrenovic is recorded as addressing -- and it says: "Can I talk to Jevdjevic? "K: Sure." And then O says: "Hello Jevdo? Now, we see the reference is to Jevdo. What comment do you have on the use of this nickname, which is different from the nickname in the intercept that was referred to by the Prosecution, and it is the Defence position that it is different from that which is on the audio recording of the same. What comment do you have on the purported use of that nickname by Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two completely different nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did Obrenovic frequently use or ever use the nickname that is reflected in the document before us now, Jevdo, when addressing yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody called me that, him included.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to the theoretical ability for both ends of a conversation to be heard on one channel by way of leakage from the headset to the microphone. You said at transcript page 32111 that this was very complicated and required agreement of technical preconditions. Did your answer to Ms. Hasan explore all of the technical difficulties that would mitigate against such leakage resulting in a useable full conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That question actually misstates the question I put to the witness and the witness's testimony. In fact, the witness was -- testified about complicated and technical ways that two participants can be heard on one frequency, and then we moved on to a very simple method which was via the telephone set and the -- the voice moving into the microphone and travelling through the one frequency, and the witness agreed that that was a simple method by which both participants could be heard on the frequency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- apparently there's some difference of view of what the evidence is. Could you guide me to the relevant page and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 32111 is the one I have written down, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 32111, there is no question put by Ms. Hasan to the witness. It was questioning by Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at 32112. The question begins at line 7. Well, in fact -- yes, at line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- just one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, my mouse is malfunctioning, so I cannot assist in terms of navigating, so I'm grateful to Your Honour and to opposing counsel for assisting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just re-read what the evidence was. Yes, the answer is not entirety without ambiguity. After the witness had explained what complications there were to make such an intercept, it was put to the witness by Ms. Hasan that the leakage system, if I could call it that, is a very simple explanation. And then the witness praised Ms. Hasan by saying, well, you more or less summed it up nicely. And in -- he then explained that it sometimes is difficult to hear one of the interlocutors. And then he continued: "If anybody wants to listen to technical explanations, I can give them to you. It's not necessarily directly linked to the complex situation in the technical intercepts." That's what the evidence appears to be. Could you please rephrase your question and be very precise as to whether you want a technical explanation on the leakage or the non-leakage intercept method.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the leakage scenario presented, could you give us a technical description of the power output levels of the receiver headset as compared to the transmitting mouthpiece or microphone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please just repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the leakage scenario that was presented of audio leaking from the headset into the receiver's microphone, could you give us a technical description of the -- or comparison of the power level outputs of the receiver headset as well as the ability of the transmitting mouthpiece or microphone to receive sounds.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a technical point of view, that is negligible power of the transmission signal that comes from the headset because the weakening is not limitless. It is a negligibly small quantity of the signal that gets to the microphone, and then the microphone can transmit a negligible quantity of signal further on. In order to intercept such a conversation, the interception station has to be very close to one of the transmission relays. There has to be optical visibility, and the antenna has to be directed between the two participants involved in order to use that tiny bit of power that goes from the headset to the microphone that we ordinary users of telephones cannot register at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've said that an interception centre has to be very close. Are you able to provide any more precision in terms of the use of that term "very close," let's say, in terms of the optimal range of a transmitter?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the rules for intercepting radio relay and other communications, the planning always is that the interception posts should be as close as possible to the enemy and the enemy front line, because in that way it is easier to intercept these conversations and immerse what comes from their devices, because what is counted on is that the enemy is also operating with devices with less power. If I have already said that at all the radio relay routes that are shorter than 20 or 25 metres [As interpreted], we always used half of the power involved, and we had many such situations, that means that electromagnetic waves in this technical range of 50 kilometres is halved. So the interpretation post has to be very nearby in terms of kilometres. It has to have optical visibility with the transmitter of the enemy, and the antenna has to be directed at the beam between the two participants in the enemy conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have just been recorded as saying that for "radio relay routes that are shorter than 20 or 25 metres, we always used half of the power involved." Did you in fact mean 20 to 25 metres or some other measure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My last few questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a follow-up question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm totally lost here, Witness. I understand that the level, the volume level of the sound that reaches the microphone, that that is very low. If it leaks somewhere, I have, however, great difficulties in understanding how that influences the power of the radio signal sent. Wouldn't it be that even if it's very difficult to hear it that it would travel the guaranteed distance on the radio relay path? Because you are -- as far as I understand, you say if the sound is very low, that it would be the same if you would speak very softly. Would that have any influence on where you could intercept that soft speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not the category of soft speech. That is just part of the electromagnetic signal that comes from the headset, because the weakening between the headset and the microphone is not limitless; that is to say, there is not a total barrier because electronic equipment is imperfect and the signal weakens from the headset to the microphone. So a small part of the signal that the human ear cannot hear comes from the headset to the microphone, and then through the microphone it goes to the transmission side; that is to say, when I'm speaking, they hear me from out there, and then we they are speaking, again, with a very weakened signal that comes from the headset and goes to the microphone, it again is transmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I all understand that, but what I do not understand that if it is then sent over the radio relay path, that it would lose its -- its force, it would lose its power earlier than what is properly and easily detected by the microphone. I -- I still have difficulties in understanding that. Because at whatever level it reaches the microphone, from there, it is sent with the same power as speech, loud speech, soft speech, whatever, then I'm -- have missed the point and could you please explain to me how that happens. And could you also explain to me: You assume that the leakage is through waves, not being sound. If I, for example, would use a system which would allow some sound to leak off that could reach the microphone as well, would that be impossible? These are my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In essence - in essence - what leaks is sound that then further on through the system turns into an electromagnetic wave. And then if you are speaking softly -- or if you are speaking more loudly, if you speak more loudly the other person will hear you better. If you speak softly, then the other person will barely hear you or - or - will not hear you at all. Well, you have seen here. That's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all fine. But you say it leaks as sound. Now, whether sound is leaking or whether sound is produced by a voice at that point in time, does it make any less sound which is caught by the microphone? And you explain to us that in order to intercept that, if I could say that sound which is relatively weak, you need to be closer to the sending relay station, which I do not understand because the voice or any sound leaking into the microphone would have no impact. The volume of that would have no impact on the path itself, unless you would accept that the strength of the signal would already diminish considerably on short range, but that would affect -- that would affect soft speaking as well. And I did understand that the -- that the equipment would guarantee for a more or less quality relay over the distance for which it qualifies, which you said could be down at half, but I do not understand why that sound would be more difficult apart from that it is at a different volume that you would need to be closer for an intercept than any other sound that would reach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very simply, the power of the sound determines the range or the distance it will go. The power of the signal does that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever a microphone catches is sent at the level of power the equipment allows for. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would. If you speak aloud, then you use more decibels, more power, the range is bigger. And then if you speak softly, then you use less decibels, you use less power, and the distance the sound travels is shorter, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand that the quality of the signal is guaranteed over the distance the equipment is made for. That means soft speaking or sound leaking into the microphone would be equally difficult to hear at the distance of 5 kilometres, 10 kilometres, 20 kilometres, depending on the power used in sending that signal. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sound that leaks from the receiver to the microphone cannot be even called soft speech because we can't hear it. It goes to the microphone as a signal that is inaudible to the human ear. But the microphone is also an amplifier. It amplifies it and sends it to the receiving end. The amplification, however, is not good enough so as to be heard at all ranges. If the interception station is close enough, it can pick it up and it can hear it. If not, then no. That's why there are a lot of intercepted conversations where it says the other speaker is not heard, the other interlocutor is not heard. We've had that in this courtroom as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that we're at or beyond the time for a break. I have one area of -- a handful of questions. Two questions, I think, is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would take approximately how much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I leave it in your own hands whether you want to use these five minutes and then to conclude your re-examination or -- and perhaps also having consulted with your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My client has greed to proceed. I don't know about the booths if they have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Ms. Hasan, how much time as matters stand now, you would need? If no surprises come up in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Approximately 30 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately 30 minutes. Then it still may be good to finish this so that Ms. Hasan is better able to organise her --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on that matter, I have a medical appointment that's been planned for about two months that I have to make. Now, I'm prepared to stay if you would like me to do the re-examination. We've spoken to the Defence about Mr. McCloskey doing any -- sorry, re-cross, and the Defence has agreed. But I'm in your hands as to whether I have permission to leave or whether I should stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As long as you guarantee that Mr. McCloskey also stays within the 30 minutes. That's -- that would be more of a concern than any other matter at this moment. If there's a commitment, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware that Mr. McCloskey has been present during the whole of the examination of this witness, as far as we remember, and for that reason the Chamber does not object to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ivetic, if you would finish your re-examination in the next five minutes, then we'd take a break after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If we can have P338. And when we get there, it will be page 43 in the English, page 39 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the second full -- the first full paragraph, the second paragraph on the page in English, and you were asked about a special problem: "Is the large number of privately owned means of communication in the brigades and lower tactical units the so-called Motorolas which cannot be controlled as well as the undisciplined radio communications of operating staff?" Now I want to ask you, in so far as this refers to the brigades and lower tactical levels, does this apply to radio relay devices or radio devices?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio device, ham radios; not military devices. We used to call them Motorolas in our military jargons, or UKT devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now as to radio devices within the Drina Corps, were the frequencies of those changed during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those frequencies changed. It depended on the units because those devices were used by a lower-ranking tactical units. Everybody changed frequencies as they planned, and they worked within a different frequency spectrum in comparison with radio relay devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the standard radio device used at the tactical level, what was the range of transmission for, let's say, a RUP-12?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no such thing as a RUP-80. Any other interpretation of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: RUP-12.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The range of a RUP-12 that we most commonly used at lower tactical levels was it between 12 -- 2 and 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for answering my questions. I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, one thing I do have to put on the record: We looked at P1633, the intercept that had the Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic and had the Jevdo nickname. I want to bring to Your Honours' attention that P1662 purports to be the same intercept, again referring to Obrenovic as lieutenant-colonel or colonel and the Jevdo nickname, and also P1661 is again that version of the intercept without any rank for Obrenovic but still using the Jevdo nickname; whereas, P1398 and P1397, which the Prosecution has used, neither have the rank in issue nor the nickname but they all purport to come from the same source, the ABiH, and to be drafted in August of 1995. It has been and remains the position of the Defence that the ABiH doctored and/or fabricated intercepts after the war to suit their needs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We very briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you'll -- as you may have understood from what happened before the break, you'll now be further examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
