utterances.text: Colonel, good afternoon. It's been some time.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to take us to 65 ter 04328, and I'll remind us of the August 2nd intercept which was P0137, that's the conversation with General Krstic saying "kill them all" to Obrenovic and the Cowboys. I think we'll recall that Obrenovic said in that intercept that: "We've managed to catch a few more, either on gunpoint or on mines." And with that mind, I hope we'll see this document which should be the day before the intercept. It's a regular combat report from the Zvornik Brigade. It's in the name of -- excuse me, of Pandurevic, which we can't see in the English but I think we can take my -- hopefully my word for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't we go to the second page. Okay. And let's go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would refer us all to the third paragraph under point number 1 -- sorry. Paragraph number 1 -- point number 1, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it should say: "In the early hours of the morning, a small group of enemy soldiers stumbled into an mp ..." Is that minefield?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "... in front of the 7th Infantry Battalion's trenches in the Pandurica area, where a few Muslim soldiers were left dead and wounded." So that roughly corresponds to the intercept of the following day, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is about the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it a practice to leave wounded soldiers on a minefield to die?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't practice that and I never heard from anybody that something like that happened in other units. It all depended on whether they were accessible. In any case, I never heard about that being common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 04328 receives number P7147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You spoke briefly about Zvonko Bajagic and that he was a devout person that was at this dinner that you've talked about, and that he brought fish to the dinner at the Bratunac Brigade. And I can tell you it's the Prosecution's position that there was fish served at the Bratunac Brigade at that dinner; however, as you understand, it's the Prosecution's position that that dinner happened on the 12th. Now, let me read you a question and an answer that Zvonko Bajagic gave in the Popovic trial, and the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have that transcript on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If possible. We just dug this up. I didn't know it would be this quick -- I'd be able to do it this quickly. It seems like a long time ago. And this was in March 2009. If we could down, there we go. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see, and this the Prosecutor, Mr. Mitchell, saying: "Sir, it's the Prosecution's position that we've proven beyond a reasonable doubt that this meeting and the dinner at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters happened on the evening of the 12th of July, and that you are not telling the truth as you sit here today." This is Mr. Bajagic's answer: "You say what you want. How could it have been on the 12th? On the 12th was the day when you were supposed to eat meat. This would be like not eating meat on Christmas or asking me if I eat meat at Christmas or not, if I eat fish at Christmas."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's at page 32535.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he says that you're supposed to eat meat on the 12th, not fish, I take it, and -- but isn't it very possible, sir, that in this situation, on the 12th, fish was served?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object. It misstates the evidence both of this witness and the evidence that's being presented from the Popovic case as to it not being the 12th, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just -- one second, please. Well, I don't see any misstatement of the evidence. I re-read it. The question simply is: Even if you would expect to eat meat on the 12th, wouldn't it still be possible to eat fish? That's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's position, and you're invited to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be totally against our customs. The fasting period is several weeks long, and then on the 12th we serve meat like we do on Christmas, so it would be completely contrary to our Orthodox customs to have somebody serve fish on the 12th. Impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're saying it's not possible that you had fish on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not eat fish. As soon as General Mladic gave me my orders --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I went through the door and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have much time left. You've gotta -- I'm just saying, is it not possible that they had fish on the 12th, is that what you're saying, because of your customs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a clue what happened in Srebrenica on the 12th because I left Bratunac at 2300 hours on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you would be very surprised if I showed you a video of Zvonko Bajagic hosting General Mladic and others on the 12th of July, Saint Petrov's Day, with a huge tableful of fish. That would surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be totally contrary to our customs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the trial video P01147. I'll try to make this short. It's V000-9266. We'll start at 00:30:09.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the church in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not paying too much attention to the interior, but I do recognise Zvonko Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where he is in this -- in this shot?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is in the middle of this frame and he's holding a cake in his hands together with one of the church dignitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's keep playing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was at 30 -- 30:09.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll try to skip ahead a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person with the hat?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's keep watching. At 00:31:16.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he's to our back, but did you see Zvonko Bajagic come into this shot?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's his back facing us now at --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's position that that's fish.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like fish to me too, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So perhaps Zvonko Bajagic isn't as religious as you thought?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Orthodox faith, on two days in the week, on Wednesday and on Friday -- if that 12th of July was either a Wednesday or a Friday -- there are two days a week when non-meat food is served during religious ceremonies. So if the 12th of July 1995 was either a Wednesday or a Friday, and if that was shot on that day, that may be the explanation. That's the only explanation I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's explanation that you are lying, that Bajagic is lying, that Krstic was lying, that Andric lied, that all the commanders that went to this meeting are lying about this for the reasons stated by Ms. Hasan because of what was going on in Bratunac on the 12th of July. Do you consider that perhaps you are just mistaken because you weren't there, or do you want to join this lie for your final time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object to this question as it's phrased, especially the last part. At this point, Mr. McCloskey is harassing the witness. He is compounding the question with asking allowable questions and disallowable questions, and I think it's a highly inappropriate manner of questioning this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think there is some merit in what Mr. Ivetic brings to our attention. If you would adopt the style used by Ms. Hasan, you might be just as effective. And since you are replacing her, I would suggest you do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can't even try to do that, Mr. President, but I think we can go on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We stopped at 32:02.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think no -- has a question been put to the witness at this moment? No. Wait for the next question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have another -- an explanation you want to give?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to adopt your style and I'm not going to tell you if you are lying when you say that I am lying. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please refrain from those kind of comments. I think, based on the objection by Mr. Ivetic, we took care that you'll not be harassed or intimidated, if that was the case. Would you please refrain from using that language towards one of the counsel in this courtroom. Just not acceptable. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said what I knew about the interpretation of that possibility. If the 12th of July was either a Wednesday or a Friday, it is possible that the church dignitaries who were fasting on that day were served fish irrespective of the fact that it was still a fasting period. It is a common practice in the Orthodox faith that people eat fish or, rather, they don't eat meat on Wednesdays and Fridays, and this is my only explanation, the only one that I've had throughout my whole testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you recognise this to be inside Zvonko Bajagic's house and not the church property?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the beginning, you asked me whether I recognised the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question. We've seen in the footage a certain ceremony in the church. Would that ceremony be the ceremony of Saint Peter's Day or would that be a ceremony which was held at the last day of the fasting period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That ceremony is typical of Saint Peter's Day, that is also the day of that church in Vlasenica, and when that is celebrated, there's usually a typical cake which is broken by people in the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do I understand, then, that the -- your recollection that fish was eaten doesn't mean that it wasn't a fasting period but it could well be after the fasting period, for example, on Saint Peter's Day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 11th of July is the last day of fasting and fasting had to be observed. On all other days, true Christian Orthodox believers, even if it is not a fasting period related to a big holiday, they will always eat fish or at least no meat on Wednesdays and Fridays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, them eating fish would still allow for the possibility if the 12th of July was -- no. I leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. There was some discussion about this idea or this process where the sound coming in to the earphone of a telephone can leak or go into the mouthpiece. Is this more likely to happen if you're holding the telephone away from your head so that the earphone is not tightly up against your head?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you a -- a video-clip of General Mladic. He's speaking on a -- I believe it's a RUP device. It's not a RRU-1 or an RRU-800, and I'm not attempting to confuse the two, and I know they're operating differently and they're intercepted differently. This is a simplex machine. But you'll see when you see the video that he is holding the telephone away from his head and he is speaking into it, and we're watching a video and we're hearing the sound of General Mladic speak, and we're also hearing the sound of -- of the person that's speaking into the earphone -- or speaking out of the earphone to General Mladic. It's -- it's Colonel Andric, as a matter of fact. So I want to show that to you and see if this is what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have 65 ter 26123a. It should be very short, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. All right. Well, that's -- we don't have the complete piece, so I think we'll just to have leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we just saw that. I don't know if we can still that picture. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if the camera that's filming this can pick up the earpiece that Mladic has got near his ear, can't we conclude that if the video camera picking up the sound coming out of that earpiece, can't we conclude in that case the mouthpiece that General Mladic would be speaking into would also pick up that sound?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a completely different operating principle. It's called simplex. It would mean that while I'm speaking, you're listening. When I finish, then I let the button go, and it is only then that my ear piece can be activated so that I can hear the other side. This sound absolutely cannot be transmitted because simplex communications absolutely imply that only one participant can be heard and nobody else can be heard within that network for as long as one participant is speaking. For as long as he keeps the button pressed, no one else can be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with you and I'm not asking about that. If this was duplex where you don't have to say "over and out," that two people can speak at the same time, over each other sometimes, if that's the case, can't the sound coming out of the earpiece go right into the mouthpiece just like it's going into the video machine that we can hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object that there's been a lack of foundation laid as to whether this is the same set-up that would be expected from a duplex machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's not the -- I think Mr. McCloskey clearly explained that that's not the issue. The simple question is, I think -- yes, the objection is denied. The simple question is whether if this camera can catch audible sound at such a distance, whether that would not be possible to be caught by a microphone at a similar distance. That means incoming signals being audible even at this distance with this equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This equipment is constructed in such a way that it is impossible from the signal from the receiving end to go further. Otherwise, you can hear that from here to where you are. Not only I, but you and everybody in the courtroom can hear that so well. It's so audible, so loud. But the equipment is constructed in such a way that on the other side, nothing can be relayed. Nothing can be transmitted. This is a completely different piece of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and as I said, I agree with that. And that's the safety device for the simplex built in. But when you're speaking on a similar telephone, from a RRU-800, it's a different system, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a different -- RRU-800 is different. You can -- you don't have to say "over and out," and it could go from the earphone to the mouthpiece, as I think I've already testified in previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sound does not go to the microphone through the air. It goes electrically through the interior of the -- of the receiver, and then it is amplified and goes further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm told we can see the clip, which I think will help us a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could try to find that clip. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It's the same video. We'll just start from 00:20:30.0.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think we stop at 00:20:53.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you hear the -- the voice of the person coming out of Mladic's earphone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is characteristic of simplex communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And so if the microphone and the videocamera that caught this, the -- the -- the -- the mouthpiece of the telephone would also have caught it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As if we were using this equipment here in court, we would all hear both participants, both interlocutors. There is no microphone there. It's just like these police devices. You had the opportunity of seeing that in town. When one policeman is talking to another one, you never have an opportunity to hear the other policeman until the one that you see releases the button and gives him that possibility. Until he frees the transmission, if you will. Because there is no separate channel for reception and separate for transmission. It's just one channel: Simplex. And it's busy while one person is talking. Once he releases and when he releases the button, it is only then that the other person can speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask one question. How do you know that what we just saw in the video that that was simplex communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I know what the device is and according to which principle it works. I learned that at school. It is a RUP-12, and it's range from 2 to 12 kilometres, and it's up to 1.8 watt and so on and so forth. So I know the principles of how it operates. It operates like police equipment: While one person is speaking, nobody else can speak. While I'm speaking, I cannot hear anyone else. It is only when I release that channel, then I can hear others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understood that. Let me put one additional question: Does the duplex communication look differently from what we saw in the -- in the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Duplex is what you and I are involved in now, that we're speaking. We can hear each other as we speak. And simplex is you cannot say anything to me while I'm talking. I simply cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not my question. Could you see in the video that this was simplex and not duplex communication? Could you see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Because when General Mladic is communicating his order, then he releases the button. He frees the channel so that he can get a response. Focus on his hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's no disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does the device look differently? I'm not talking about the movement of the hand of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a completely different kind of device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These of are very small power and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I'm getting a bit lost, and I'm just verifying with you, Mr. McCloskey, whether I understand your line of questioning well, that it's exclusively focusing on whether you can hear sound coming in on an earphone or at least an ear part irrespective of any other technical aspects of the communication. Is that what you were asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. Because I agree with everything else he's saying. We can see it's a simplex, we know it's a simplex, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Witness, the only matter that was raised by Mr. McCloskey was whether if you use an earphone in whatever situation whether sometimes what is the incoming sound is audible at some distance. Here I think it is approximately 1 or 2 metres. Audible sound. That was the issue raised. Do you agree that that is possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is absolutely possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would like to -- yes, no, I will leave that for a later moment, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, if I showed you a photo of a -- well, you'll agree with me that a RRU-1 can be held on the back and is portable like you've already said; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the telephone for the RRU-1 is close to or identical in appearance to the telephone that we just saw in Mladic's hand?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That device does not have a telephone. It just has a micro-telephone combination; however, this here is a RUP-12 through which General Mladic is speaking. That was in the photograph that was shown a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I got a photograph of a RUP-1 and the phone to me looks exactly like the one Mladic is holding. Isn't the one right now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get it up so we can see what Mladic is holding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you'll keep track on what you're showing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So here we at 00:20:39.9. This -- let's call it a -- I don't know what you call it. A hand -- a handpiece. It's green on the bottom and black at the top. Is this pretty much the way the phone or the handpiece from a RRU-1 looks like?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a telephone. This is a micro-telephone combination that is connected to equipment. This is not a telephone. You and other people who don't know this call this a receiver. This is a micro-telephone combination, professionally speaking, and it is attached to this equipment. You see it up here. There's no telephone here. There's just this combination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this micro-telephone that Mladic is holding the same micro-telephone -- does it appear be to the same on a RRU-1?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are similar but RRU-1 operates in duplex, and you can never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's not the issue raised by Mr. McCloskey at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You earlier in your testimony suggested that we could do a forensic analysis of the printouts from the Pribicevac forward command post from your machine that you carried around with you and the machines at the Drina Corps. Well, we -- we did that years ago, and I have a -- I have a report that I've provided the Defence, and it has somewhat of a conclusion, and I -- at this point, I'm not sure I want to argue with you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if you're interested in hearing anymore about it, but I do have an expert report. I could read in the conclusion or I'm also at -- we'll see what Mr. Ivetic has got to say about this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm inquiring if you have one that is signed? The one that you gave me yesterday is unsigned, so...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My guess we do have a signed report, and it is an official expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. On the basis of that assumption, yes, I leave it to you, Mr. McCloskey, how you want to proceed. Of course, the Chamber is always interested in receiving whatever evidence that improves our ability to -- to evaluate the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I will leave that -- yes. If I could try to read the conclusion, and it's 65 ter 32125. And this is -- can be complicated, so I don't expect us to be able to resolve anything in our question and answer, but I think it will be helpful. And at the end where it says "assessment of the evidence." And this is a situation where this person was given the originals of the materials that came from the Pribicevac forward command post and some examples that came from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can correct, Mr. McCloskey. I believe that the individual in question complained about the fact that one of the documents was a copy, not the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One -- yeah, that's true. One was a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes, did that lead to any conclusion that it could not be examined in such a way as to draw conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's what she said about that one but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That one, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And many others, and I think we'll get the gist of this. "Assessment of the evidence. The assessment of the evidence I have found in this case depends upon whether it has to be considered that any ETL-1 printer that was produced with a similar typeface to the questioned and specimen documents submitted could have been used to produce the questioned typescript, or whether only the printers at Pribicevac or Drina Corps Command could have been used. "In the former scenario, the evidence is such that whilst there are similarities between the questioned typescripts (in both original and copy form) and the specimens from Pribicevac printer number [sic] 1, these defects are insufficient to show that it was this printer rather than any other similar ETL-1 printer that was used to produce the documents in question. There is, however, in my opinion some limited evidence to show that this printer was responsible. In addition, there is some evidence to show that the questioned documents were not produced by the printers at the Drina Corps Command whose specimens had been submitted. "If, however, only the printers at the two sites could have produced the questioned documents, then the questioned typescript corresponds more closely with the specimens from Pribicevac printer number 1, especially the specimens dated 11/7/95 and 12/7/95, than those from the Drina Corps Command and thus there is in my opinion strong evidence that this printer produced the questioned documents." And she goes on at the end of her report where she has four grades basically for her assessments. One is conclusive evidence, this may be positive or negative; two is strong but not conclusive evidence, this may be positive or negative; three, limited evidence, this may be positive or negative; four, inconclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give any brief comment, if you can? It's the Prosecution's position that this is fundamentally saying there's evidence that that the items that came out of the Pribicevac, according to the Prosecution, 11 and 12 July, came from one printer, your printer, and that it didn't look like it was the Drina Corps printer, but it's not conclusive. What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to carry out any kind of valid expertise an expert, first of all, has to have original documents. Every copy disrupts the letters as typed on the teleprinter, and there has to be a sufficient number of documents in order to carry out a valid analysis; that is to say, copies are absolutely out of the question. Furthermore, one should focus on the following. In the command of the Drina Corps, we had three or four printers, but at the IKM only one. I still maintain and I'm absolutely certain that the teleprinter that was used at the IKM is not -- actually, that those documents, those two documents that you showed me during the cross-examination were not printed there, and I'm certain of that from many aspects. And my entire testimony over the past 15 years has attested to that, starting with the one that I conducted with your investigator Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President I would offer this into evidence. It -- well, I won't -- have another one. It's a signed version, so we'll -- it's being uploaded now, I guess, and it's 32125a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If it's being presented as an expert opinion to the truth of the matters asserted therein, I believe its tendering right now is in violation of Rule 94 bis. The Defence would object to it being tendered through this witness, and we would -- and would request that the Rule 94 bis procedure be adhered, and in this case it would require the Prosecution asking to reopen their case to present positive evidence of their position which has now been succinctly stated by Mr. McCloskey and that we be given appropriate time to -- to deal with the 94 bis procedure and to address that expert opinion that has not been previously presented. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, primary objection: Violation of Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, as you -- as we all saw, this witness under the questioning of -- of Mr. Ivetic is the one that made the very unusual comment and basically asked us or suggested to us that we do this test, and that it would show a particular result. This is called kicking the adversarial door wide open, and once do you that then the Prosecution can bring forward this kind of material. I believe in this Tribunal, you -- it is in the discretion of the Trial Chamber under 54 bis and other Rules that in this particular very unique context, you can bring this in and it's a matter of weight. And this has been something that was brought up by them. I -- and so we're filling in the gap that they created. There was no objection to getting this far with it. The objection comes after all the testimony comes in. Any objection should have been before this, not that we have now seen this evidence. I think now it's incumbent upon the Trial Chamber to be able to look at this evidence and study it if they want or cast it aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if I could ask you one question in this context: You're arguing that Rule 54 bis would be the -- would give the Chamber power to order anything. So, for example, is it your position also that we could deviate from Rules of Procedure and Evidence adopted by the Judges for trial just by using 54 bis, for example, to say, well, we -- tomorrow we'll accept a 92 bis statement without an attestation or going to the act of and conduct of the accused? Would that be possible, in your view, under Rule 54 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not under the examples you just gave. But -- and I'm not suggesting this is the catch all, I would not do that, that would, of course, not be correct, it would damage the Prosecution and the Tribunal. Though I have seen, and I think justifiably so, that 92 [sic] bis has not disallowed portions of particular statements to come into evidence, for example. And that has, I think, been done under the discretion of Trial Chambers in this institution for quite a while, and I wouldn't limit myself to 54 bis. I'm sure there are other Rules and cases that I could get you and to help -- help clarify this issue. But I do think when unique situations like this come up, that it provides the Trial Chamber with a unique ability to do what they think is most fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could only just add one thing -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before I give you an opportunity to add something, the Chamber is about to invite the parties to make written submissions on the admissibility of expert reports as presented today, and would mark the expert report for identification for the time being. Does that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That obviates the need for me to make any further submissions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That doesn't fully surprise me. Then the parties are invited to make written submissions within 14 days on the admissibility of the expert report in the way it was presented in this courtroom. Now, one final -- yes, a number should be assigned. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the signed one uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Two minutes is the estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then if you reserve a number for it, and then the signed version will be uploaded soon and is then marked for identification. Under what number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P7148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And under what number would the signed version be uploaded?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As far as I understand, Your Honours, it would be 3125a, but I kindly ask that it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be confirmed. Now I have a final question for the parties: Is there any agreement on the day of the 12th of July, 1995? Whether that was a -- which day of the week it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have checked, and perhaps counsel can also check and confirm, but I have it as a Wednesday, according to unofficial sources, of course, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll check. We haven't checked. I have no reason to doubt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should be fully transparent. I looked at a calendar in -- on the Internet which also dates the 12th of July as a Wednesday, 12th of July, 1995. Just on the basis of this assumption, I have another question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you argued in quite some detail that the fact that you ate fish during that meeting that that demonstrates that it must have been within the fasting period of which the last day was the 11th of July. Now, if the parties would agree on the 12th of July being a Wednesday, would that deprive most of the -- of the compelling character of concluding that it must have been the 11th because you ate fish, because on the 12th, if that was a Wednesday? I do understand it's quite traditional to eat fish as well.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the meeting which was on the 11th, they had fish because it was part of the obligatory fasting. As for the ceremony, personally Bishop Kacavenda was present. I met him, I know him. He was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you not whether you ate fish on the 11th. I'm asking you whether what you presented to us as a compelling logic that it must have been the 11th because you ate fish, that that has lost quite some of its compelling character because it would be as traditional to eat fish on Wednesday, the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm afraid that I do not understand why the fish would still point at the 11th and could not have been eaten on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The religious fasting, which lasts for several weeks, ends on the 11th. Everybody eats fish on that day. However, the most devout believers, like Bishop Kacavenda and others, also eat fish on Wednesdays and Fridays, as a matter, of course, even outside of the fasting periods. That's why I assume, since Bishop Kacavenda was in the gentleman's house for lunch, that he could eat fish after the 11th only if those -- if that was either a Wednesday or a Friday, and I'm very pleased that you have now confirmed that that day, indeed, was a Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware that you're changing your testimony? Earlier you said it was unimaginable that someone on the 12th would eat fish and that was at the basis of your conclusion that it must have been the 11th. And now you're explaining to us that you're quite happy to hear that the 12th was a Wednesday on which religious people would certainly -- would possibly eat fish. Are you aware that this is a switch, that this is a change in your -- what you presented as compelling logic? I'm just asking whether you're aware of it. A simple yes or no would do.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We got the number slightly wrong or the Registry did. It's 32125a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said you needed two minutes? Two minutes are over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's there. Then 32125a is the document now uploaded, the signed version of an expert report which was marked for identification. Mr. Jevdjevic, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answered all questions that were put to you, many questions put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And good-bye to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer to proceed after the break with a few court agenda items rather than to start the testimony of the next witness. If that is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then can I ask for him to be released through VWS? Is that -- I understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- at least, unless there are compelling reasons to start his testimony today, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would defer to Mr. Stojanovic because he's the one working with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is nothing. I would just like to release the witness with our apologies because he's been here since 11.00 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would indeed be good to apologise to the witnesses on whomever's behalf, there's no one guilty, perhaps, but it's a pity that he had to wait for such a long time. We will take a break, we'll resume at ten minutes to 2.00, and we'll then deal primarily are procedural matters, agenda items. I have a long list. We take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few agenda items I'd like to get rid of. But perhaps before I start with the first item, a matter was raised by Mr. Ivetic this morning about the handwritten words "Mladic" added in the English version of P1657 and P1658. I tried for myself to clarify whether the original B/C/S was part of both of these exhibits. I had some doubts. If the Prosecution would please have a look at it to see whether there is any possible error involved. Then I -- my first item is an instruction regarding a colour version of Exhibit P999. On the 18th of February, 2015, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence via e-mail that it had located and uploaded into e-court a colour version of P999 tendered through Nermin Karagic on the 21st of February, 2013. The Chamber hereby instructing the Registry to replace the black-and-white version of P999 with the colour version uploaded under document ID 0216-6225-A. The next item deals with P6682. On the 15th of January, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence, again via an e-mail, that it had received B/C/S translations for P6682, a document which had been admitted into evidence on the 17th of December, 2014. Further, the Prosecution requested that if the Defence was in agreement, the Court Officer should be instructed to attach the translation and that the document be admitted. I do not know whether there's any objection from the Defence side to these translations. I hear of no objections, and there's always a possibility to revisit the matters within 48 hours. But the Chamber refers the parties to its decision on admission of P6682, which was delivered in court on the 17th of December of last year and the relevant instruction to the Registry contained therein, and this can be found at transcript pages 30029 through 30031. Next item is an issue remaining from the testimony of Slobodan Zupljanin. On the 2nd of February 2015 during the testimony of Slobodan Zupljanin, P7090 was marked for identification pending receipt of the official English translation. This can be found at transcript page 30966. The Prosecution informed the Chamber on the 3rd of February via e-mail that a revised translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID number 0041-5655-ET and requested that, first, the Chamber instruct the Registry to replace the existing translation with the revised version; and, second, to admit P7090 into evidence. The Defence informed the Chamber on the 7th of February via e-mail that it objected to the revised translation. The Chamber reminds the Defence that it can seek verification of the translation with CLSS, if it still objects to the translation. The Chamber hereby admits P7090 into evidence, and instructs the Registry to replace the current translation of P7090 with the document bearing document ID number 0041-5655-ET. I repeat that if there's still other problems with the translation, of course they can be addressed. The next item deals with evidence which potentially overlaps with agreed facts. On the 19th of November, 2014, the Defence filed 92 ter motions for Bosiljka Mladic, Radovan Popovic, Biljana Stojkovic, and Zarko Stojkovic. The Prosecution does not oppose the motions. On the 19th of January of this year, the Chamber asked the Defence to indicate why it deemed it necessary to present evidence from witnesses in relation to facts that have already been agreed between the parties pursuant to the joint submission on agreed facts dated the 4th of June 2013; namely, the accused's whereabouts between the 14th and the 17th of July, 1995. The Defence advised the Chamber that there are three items in dispute: First, whether or not the accused had any means of communication by which he was able to command his forces; second, the time of the accused's return to Republika Srpska; and, third, the accused's whereabouts on the 16th of July, 1995. And this can be found at transcript pages 30156 through 30158. Following the Defence's submissions, the Chamber has reviewed the four 92 ter motions and is satisfied that the Defence intends to present evidence that has not been dealt with in the 4th of June, 2013 filing. I move to my next item dealing with the issue remaining from the testimony of Vojo Kupresanin. I should say "issues" rather than "issue." During the testimony of Vojo Kupresanin in December 2014, the Prosecution tendered various lengthy documents which were marked for identification pending agreement between the parties as to the excerpts to be admitted. On the 26th of January of this year, the Prosecution advised the Defence and the Chamber, via e-mail, that it had uploaded excerpts of P6997, P7000, P7002, P7003, and P7005 under 65 ter numbers 08469a, 05995a, 02335a, 02337a, and 02345a respectively. On the 7th of February, the Defence advised the Chamber and the Prosecution via e-mail that it did not object to the admission of these excerpts. The Registry is hereby instructed to replace P6997 with 65 ter 08469a, P7000 with 65 ter 05995a, P7002 with 65 ter 02335a, P7003 with 65 ter 02337a, and P7005 with 65 ter 02345a and admits them into evidence. In relation to the remaining associated exhibits for Vojo Kupresanin, the Chamber invites the Defence to respond to the Prosecution's filing of informal communication regarding this witness's associated exhibits no later than the 27th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the time-limit I just said was drafted at least a couple of days ago, and it therefore is extended by one week. So not the 27th of February but then somewhere early March, one week later. Then the next item deals with remaining issues with regard to Exhibit D613 and 65 ter 30651. On the 23rd of January of this year, the Chamber inquired in court whether the Defence had, first, an update regarding the translation of Exhibit D613; and, second, any objections to the admission of 65 ter 30651. The Chamber notes that this inquiry was made after a number of e-mails were sent from Chamber's staff to the Defence. I refer to the 9th of December, the 16th of December, and the 17th of December. On the 23rd of January, Mr. Ivetic advised the Chamber, and I quote: "It's not one I'm working on, but I think a short deadline should suffice and I'll make sure it gets done." The Chamber then set a deadline for the following Monday, the 26th of January, and this can all be found on transcript pages 30502 through 30503. As of today's date, the Defence has not updated the Chamber regarding Exhibit D613, nor has it objected to the admission of 65 ter 30651. The Chamber interprets the Defence's continued silence with regard to 65 ter 30651 to mean that it does not object to its admission. The Chamber hereby admits 65 ter 30651 into evidence, but a number still has to be assigned. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 65 ter 30651 will receive Exhibit P7148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7148 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correction, Your Honours: 7149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7149, hereby corrected; that is, 65 ter 30651 is admitted under number P6149 -- 7149. It seems that if you make one mistake, you make many. The Chamber hereby instructs the Defence to upload into e-court a translation of Exhibit D613 no later than the 23rd of March -- I apologise, the 3rd of March, and instructs the Registry to attach the translation to the Exhibit D613. The next item deals with the remaining issue from the testimony of Cedo Sipovac. On the 12th of November, 2014, during the testimony of Cedo Sipovac, D767, D768, and D769 were marked for identification. This can be found at transcript page 28220. On the 3rd of February of this year, the Defence submitted that although it may use these documents with another witness, it would like to tender them through Sipovac to which the Prosecution objected. The Defence then stated that it would consider the admission of these documents through another witness and that it would respond later. This can be found at transcript page 31043. And the Chamber asks the Defence whether it is now in a position to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this moment, we're not. I -- Mr. Lukic, I believe, did that witness. I am transmitting a message to him as we speak, but I don't anticipate that we'll have a response for you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll expect a response from Mr. Lukic this week. Now irrespective of any decision on admission, according to an e-mail of the Defence of the 21st of January, 2015, the translations of D767, D768, and D769 have been uploaded into e-court under the following document ID numbers: 1D19-0739 for document D767; 1D19-0983 for document D768; and 1D19-0997 for document D769. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the translations to the corresponding exhibits -- documents. I move now to my next item which expresses a concern of the Chamber. The Chamber again notes, with serious concern, the reoccurring errors made by the Defence in relation to some of its 92 ter motions. The Chamber will not take the time to discuss every instance but will instead give a few relatively recent examples. First, there are inconsistencies between the numbers of associated exhibits referenced in the body of the motions and those mentioned in the request for relief or listed in the annexes. These errors can be seen in the 92 ter motions for Milenko Karisik and Milenko Zivanovic. Second, the description of the subject areas of testimony are inaccurate and even sometimes relate to a witness who is not subject of the motion. This can be seen in paragraph 10 of the 92 ter motion for Rajko Kalabic, which appears to include content related to Witness Boro Tadic. Third, the relationship between facts, evidence, and protective measures from other cases and this case are not adequately explained or provided in a timely manner. For example, during the testimony of Vinko Nikolic, a belatedly circulated concordance chart contained errors, including references to adjudicated facts that do not exist in this case. Many of these errors are consistent with the kinds of mistakes that are made when pasting content between motions without subsequently reviewing the text. In this respect, the Chamber again urges the Defence to pay closer attention to the accuracy and completeness of its motions. The Chamber also reminds the Defence that primary witness statements or transcripts from previous proceedings, tendered pursuant to Rule 92 ter, are not associated exhibits and should not be listed as such. Lastly, the Chamber reminds the Defence that it should not tender exhibits which are already in evidence. My semi-last item deals with the remaining issue from the testimony of Witness Ratko Milojica. On the 30th of September, 2014, the Defence filed a 92 ter motion for Ratko Milojica tendering his statement and four associated exhibits, and I mention the 65 ter numbers, they are: 1D03628, 1D03024, 1D03625, and 1D04969. On the 14th of October, the Prosecution filed its response not opposing the admission of Milojica's 92 ter statement but opposing the admission of two of the four associated exhibits - namely, 65 ter 1D03024 and 1D03025 - as English translations of these two documents had not been uploaded into e-court. On the 1st of December, the Chamber put on the record that the two translations had since been uploaded into e-court. This is to be found at transcript pages 29101 to 29102. The Chamber notes that the Defence did not seek admission of the four associated exhibits in court on the 1st of December. Could the Defence indicate whether this was an oversight or whether the Chamber should consider these associated exhibits to be formally withdrawn? And if no immediate answer would be available, we'd like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we believe that we will be ready to answer your question already tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the indulgence of the interpreters and all those who are assisting us, I'd like to get a clean slate for myself by reading an oral decision which is the last agenda item. The Chamber will now deliver its decision on the expertise of Ewa Tabeau in regard to the exhumation of the Tomasica mass grave. On the 26th of August, 2014, the Prosecution filed a notice of disclosure of Ewa Tabeau's expert report related to the Tomasica mass grave pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 18th of September, the Chamber granted the Defence request of the 8th of September for an extension of time to file its Rule 94 bis (B) notice. The Defence responded on the 22nd of December, objecting to the Prosecution's notice of disclosure of expert report related to the Tomasica mass grave, and the Prosecution replied on the 5th of January of this year. The Defence does not make a specific challenge to the competency of Witness Ewa Tabeau but challenges her reports as unreliable, methodologically unclear, and reaching erroneous conclusions. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October, 2012 decision concerning Richard Butler. On the basis of Tabeau's curriculum vitae, the Chamber is satisfied that she has specialised knowledge in the field of demographics. Such knowledge may be of assistance to the Chamber in understanding issues related to the evidence on the exhumation of the Tomasica grave-site. In this regard, the Chamber also notes its decision of the 7th of November, 2013, recognising Tabeau as an expert, a decision which can be found at transcript pages 18874 to -875. With regard to the Defence request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution plans to call Tabeau as part of its reopening case. The Defence will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine her. As for any of the arguments raised by the Defence related to the methodology, reliability, and exceeding of expertise of Tabeau's report, the Chamber considers that these are matters that can be and should be addressed during the cross-examination of the witness. The Defence will also have an opportunity to fully explore the witness's alleged bias in the course of cross-examination or can address it by means of an expert opinion in reply. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides pursuant to Rule 94 bis that Witness Tabeau may be recalled to testify as an expert witness and shall be made available for cross-examination by the Defence and denies the Defence request to disqualify Ewa Tabeau as an expert. The Chamber defers its decision on the admission of the report and its annexes to the time of the witness's testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Having thanked all those assisting us who granted five additional minutes, we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 25th of February, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of February, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
